items.prompt: What is a transitive dependency?
choices: A package pulled in by one of your dependencies
A package you listed yourself in package.json
A package installed only while running tests
items.explanation: A transitive dependency is one your dependencies bring in, not one you chose.

items.prompt: Who chose `case-fold` at Northfield?
choices: The platform engineer, Priya
Nobody there
The security team during an audit
items.explanation: It arrived as a dependency of `ledger-pdf`, so no one at Northfield picked it.

items.prompt: In the cafe story, what did the cafe actually vet?
choices: The sauce maker and the spice farm
Every ingredient in the jar
Only the sauce maker, one name of three
items.explanation: Only the first supplier was ever checked.

items.prompt: Which package is a direct dependency in Northfield's tree?
choices: `ledger-pdf`
`case-fold`
`font-metrics`
items.explanation: `ledger-pdf` is the library Northfield chose; the others sit behind it.

items.prompt: Compared with the packages a team reviewed, how many does a typical app install?
choices: About the same number
Many more than were reviewed
Fewer, because libraries bundle them
items.explanation: Most of the tree is transitive and never individually reviewed.

items.prompt: What can a package do automatically when you install it?
choices: Nothing until your code imports it
Only download files
Run a script, such as postinstall
items.explanation: Install scripts run without any import, which is why they matter.

items.prompt: Does approving `ledger-pdf` mean approving what it depends on?
choices: No, those names were never reviewed
Yes, approval is inherited automatically
Yes, if the library is popular enough
items.explanation: Approval covers only the name that was reviewed.

items.prompt: Why did the cafe's checklist still say 'approved' after the spice changed?
choices: The farm quietly passed its own inspection
It only listed the name that was checked
The new owner updated the cafe's list
items.explanation: The checklist tracked one name; the change happened behind it.

items.prompt: Northfield reviewed and approved `ledger-pdf`. A hostile update reaches `case-fold`, which `ledger-pdf` uses. What did the review cover?
choices: `case-fold` as well, since approval passes down the dependency tree
Nothing at all, because direct dependencies are never reviewed anywhere
`case-fold`, but only after its first install had already finished
`ledger-pdf` only; `case-fold` was never a name anyone had approved
items.explanation: Approval attaches to the names a person looked at. The review never reached the package behind the library.
items.reference:
Whose names did anyone approve?
direct dependency: chosen on purpose (`ledger-pdf`)
transitive dependency: chosen by someone else (`case-fold`)
approval covers the name you typed, not the names behind it
Why: trust flows down the tree, but review does not.
items.learnMore:
Trust you never chose

Installing a library also installs what it depends on. Every one of those packages can run code at install time or at runtime, yet only the ones you listed were ever reviewed.

Common mistake

Assuming that approving a library approves everything inside it.
items.reflection: Think of something you rely on that depends on a supplier you have never met. Whose checks are you actually relying on?

items.prompt: A team lists 12 direct dependencies and reviews them all. Their tree holds hundreds of packages. How is the unreviewed part best described?
choices: A small fringe, because libraries rarely depend on outside code
Only test tools, which never run during an install
Nothing, because the installer refuses any name nobody reviewed
Most of the code that runs, chosen by other packages' authors
items.explanation: Transitive packages make up most of a real tree, and the installer runs them without asking who reviewed them.

items.prompt: Which pattern uses a look-alike package name such as `csae-fold`?
choices: Maintainer takeover
Typosquatting
Compromised build
items.explanation: A name that looks like a popular one and relies on a typing slip is a typosquat.

items.prompt: A new owner publishes a hostile patch under the real package name. Which pattern is it?
choices: Typosquatting
Dependency confusion
Maintainer takeover
items.explanation: The real name and history are reused by a new hand.

items.prompt: Which pattern relies on a public package beating a private one with the same name?
choices: Dependency confusion
Typosquatting
Compromised build
items.explanation: The resolver picks the wrong registry's copy.

items.prompt: Which pattern leaves the source repository clean but the published package hostile?
choices: Maintainer takeover
Compromised build
Typosquatting
items.explanation: The attacker controls the machine that builds the artifact.

items.prompt: What do all four attack patterns have in common?
choices: They all exploit a bug in your code
They all need stolen passwords
You install code you did not review
items.explanation: Each one delivers hostile code through something you already trust.

items.prompt: Why can a maintainer takeover be hard to notice?
choices: The name and install history look the same
The name changes to a random string
Hostile packages always fail to install
items.explanation: Nothing about the package's identity changes.

items.prompt: Where does a dependency-confusion attacker publish?
choices: Only inside the victim's network
The public registry, under a private name
On the victim's laptop
items.explanation: A public package with the internal name can win when the resolver looks in the wrong place.

items.prompt: Why doesn't reading a repository's source rule out a compromised build?
choices: Builds never use the repository's source
Source code can't be read by tools
The published artifact may differ from the source
items.explanation: What you read and what was uploaded can be two different things.

items.prompt: A company's private registry has `acme-auth-lib` at 1.2.0. A public package of the same name appears at 9.9.9 and the build installs it. Which pattern is this?
choices: Dependency confusion
Typosquatting
Maintainer takeover
Compromised build pipeline
items.explanation: Same name, higher version, wrong registry: that is dependency confusion.
items.reference:
Four patterns, four different handles
takeover: the real name, a new hand
typosquat: a different name that looks the same
confusion: the same name, the wrong registry
compromised build: clean source, dirty artifact
Why: each pattern needs a different defence, so recognise which one you are looking at.
items.learnMore:
Naming the pattern

The useful question is what the attacker controls: a publishing account, a look-alike name, the order registries are searched in, or the build machine. The answer points to the right defence.

Common mistake

Treating all four as 'a bad package' and reaching for one tool.
items.reflection: Think of a way someone could pass off something harmful under a name you trust. Which of the four handles does it use?

items.prompt: A package's public source is clean and reviewed, yet the registry version holds an extra script. Which explanation fits best?
choices: A typosquat, because the extra script sits under a look-alike name
The build step produced an artifact different from the source
Dependency confusion, because the registry holds two copies
A takeover, because the repository history was rewritten
items.explanation: Clean source with a different published artifact points to the build, not the name or the account.

items.prompt: Which question best separates a typosquat from a maintainer takeover?
choices: Is the package written in a different language than the rest?
Is the hostile code under a different name or the real one?
Does the package have more than one listed maintainer?
Is the hostile version newer than the clean one it replaced?
items.explanation: A typosquat uses a new name; a takeover reuses the genuine one.

items.prompt: What does a vulnerability scanner compare your tree against?
choices: The package's source code line by line
Your team's code review notes
A list of problems already published
items.explanation: Scanners match versions against known, published entries.

items.prompt: A brand-new hostile release has no published entry. What does the scanner report?
choices: Nothing, it stays silent
A critical warning
A request to review the diff
items.explanation: Without an entry there is nothing to match.

items.prompt: Can a scanner flag a version before anyone has reported it?
choices: Yes, it inspects the new code
No, it has nothing to match
Yes, if it runs every hour
items.explanation: It depends on published entries, not on reading the code.

items.prompt: At 40 installs a day for 14 days, how many runs of the hostile script happen?
items.explanation: 40 multiplied by 14 is 560.

items.prompt: If detection time is halved and installs stay the same, exposure is...
choices: Halved
Unchanged
Doubled
items.explanation: Runs equal installs per day times days, so halving the days halves the runs.

items.prompt: What does scanning actually shorten?
choices: Time from 'release shipped' to 'problem exists'
Time from 'problem published' to 'we notice'
Time to write the package
items.explanation: It speeds up noticing a published problem, not the existence of one.

items.prompt: Why is a silent scanner not proof of safety?
choices: It always crashes on new versions
It only scans packages you chose directly
It only knows about published problems
items.explanation: Silence means no match, not no problem.

items.prompt: Which is the scanner's blind spot?
choices: A new hostile version nobody has reported
An old version with a published problem
A package listed twice
items.explanation: Unreported releases have nothing to match.

items.prompt: At 40 installs per day a hostile script goes undetected for 14 days. Detection improves to 7 days, installs unchanged. How many runs now?
items.explanation: Runs are 40 x 7 = 280, half of the original 560.
items.reference:
What a scanner can see
published problem list: found, flagged
brand-new hostile release: no entry, silent
40 installs per day x 14 days = 560 runs of the script
Why: a scanner matches against published entries, so it shortens the time to notice, not the time to exist.
items.learnMore:
The scanner's blind spot

A scanner can only flag a version once someone has published a problem about it. A hijacked publisher's first hostile release has no entry, so every scan before the first report returns silence.

Common mistake

Reading a clean scan as proof that nothing in the tree is hostile.
items.reflection: Think of a check you run that only knows about problems someone has already reported. What would a first-time problem look like to it?

items.prompt: Northfield starts scanning every hour. The hostile release has no published entry for three days. What does the scanner report in those days?
choices: A warning that grows each hour the version stays
A flag, because the version number is newer than before
Nothing, because it only matches published entries
A flag, because the package gained a new script
items.explanation: More frequent scans do not create an entry; the match list is what limits the scanner.

choices: A hijacked publisher's release made an hour ago
A typosquat that nobody has reported yet
A new install script in an unreported version bump
A package version reported hostile last week
items.explanation: Only already-published problems are on the list the scanner uses.

items.prompt: What does a lockfile's integrity hash fingerprint?
choices: The package's actual bytes
The maintainer's identity
The package's reputation score
items.explanation: The hash is computed over the content that was installed.

items.prompt: What does the exact version in a lockfile prevent?
choices: Every kind of hostile code
Silent drift between two installs
Anyone reading the package
items.explanation: The same lockfile resolves to the same version each time.

items.prompt: Can a lockfile say whether a version is safe?
choices: Yes, hashes exist only for safe packages
Yes, it asks the registry for a verdict
No, it only records what was chosen
items.explanation: It records and fingerprints; it does not judge.

items.prompt: Someone updates to the newest version and commits. What does the lockfile now record?
choices: The newest version and its hash
The previous clean version
A warning flag on the update, kept for review
items.explanation: It records whatever you point it at.

items.prompt: A mirror serves different bytes under the same version. What happens?
choices: The install proceeds, with a printed warning
The hash check fails and install aborts
The lockfile updates itself to match
items.explanation: A fingerprint mismatch stops the install.

items.prompt: What is a lockfile entry's job in one phrase?
choices: Decide which versions are safe to use
Remove hostile code on install
Preserve a decision, not review it
items.explanation: It keeps a choice stable over time.

items.prompt: Two installs from the same lockfile, weeks apart, get...
choices: The same versions and bytes
Whatever is newest that week
Different versions if a release came out
items.explanation: Pinning is what makes installs repeatable.

items.prompt: Does a passing integrity check show a version is trustworthy?
choices: Yes, since hostile bytes would not hash cleanly
No, only that the bytes match the record
Yes, the registry vouches for them
items.explanation: Matching bytes say nothing about whether the recorded bytes were good.

items.prompt: A teammate runs an update-to-newest command and commits the lockfile. The newest version is hostile. What does the next `npm ci` do?
choices: Aborts, because the committed hash was changed after the fact
Aborts, since newer versions need a fresh approval step
Installs the previous clean version from its cache
Installs it, since the bytes match the new lockfile entry
items.explanation: The new entry carries the hostile version's own hash, so the check passes.
items.reference:
Two jobs, neither is 'judge'
exact version: no silent drift between installs
integrity hash: same bytes as recorded
update to newest and commit: records the new version just as firmly
Why: a lockfile preserves a decision; it does not review one.
items.learnMore:
What a lockfile pins

A lockfile fixes which version each install resolves to and fingerprints the bytes. Both are facts about what was recorded, so they stay true even when the recorded version is hostile.

Common mistake

Treating a passing integrity check as a safety verdict.
items.reflection: Think of a record that only proves something is unchanged since it was written. When was it written, and who checked it then?

items.prompt: A mirror serves different bytes under version 2.3.0, which the lockfile pinned with a hash. Which feature stops it?
choices: The integrity hash, because the bytes no longer match
The exact version, because 2.3.0 is unchanged
Dependency scanning, because mirrors are all listed
The SBOM, because it names the package that was installed
items.explanation: The version number is the same; only the content fingerprint differs.

update to newest and commit: records the new version just as firmly
Why: a lockfile preserves a decision; it does not review one.

items.prompt: Which pairing of lockfile feature and risk is correct?
choices: Integrity hash with swapped bytes, exact version with silent drift
Integrity hash with silent drift, exact version with swapped bytes
Both with hostile new releases published by the real maintainer
Both with look-alike package names
items.explanation: The hash covers content; the version covers which release is resolved.

items.prompt: What is an SBOM?
choices: A list of the developers on a project
An inventory of what is inside a build
A tool that blocks hostile releases at install
items.explanation: It is a machine-readable list of components.

items.prompt: When is an SBOM generated?
choices: Only after an incident begins
Every time a file is saved
At build time, per release
items.explanation: It describes a built artifact, so it is made when that artifact is built.

items.prompt: What question does a stored SBOM answer quickly?
choices: Do we ship package X anywhere?
Is the maintainer trustworthy?
Who wrote the first commit?
items.explanation: It lists contents, so it answers membership questions.

items.prompt: Why keep old SBOMs?
choices: They make installs run faster
Old releases can get new problems
The registry deletes old versions
items.explanation: Reports about old versions keep arriving.

items.prompt: What does the dashed arrow in the pipeline mean?
choices: The build is retried if it fails
A person approves the release
Re-scan stored SBOMs later
items.explanation: New problems trigger a re-scan of what was stored.

items.prompt: Which of these is a common SBOM format?
choices: CycloneDX
Markdown
Dockerfile
items.explanation: CycloneDX and SPDX are the usual standards.

items.prompt: Without SBOMs, what do you do in an incident?
choices: Wait for the package's author to email you
Search each repository's lockfile by hand
Restart the production servers
items.explanation: That manual search is the hunt SBOMs replace.

items.prompt: Does an SBOM judge whether components are safe?
choices: Yes, it scores every package
Yes, it blocks the bad ones
No, it only lists them
items.explanation: Judging is the scanner's job.

items.prompt: A problem is published today about `case-fold` 2.4.1. Northfield has stored SBOMs for its last 20 releases. What is the quickest way to find affected releases?
choices: Rebuild each release and run its tests again
Search the stored SBOMs for that name and version
Ask each team which libraries they remember using
Scan only the latest release, since older ones are retired
items.explanation: Stored SBOMs make this a search by name and version.
items.reference:
From a hunt to a lookup
without SBOMs: open every lockfile by hand
with stored SBOMs: search by name and version
new problem published later: re-scan every stored SBOM
Why: an SBOM fixes what was inside a release, so the question can be asked again later.
items.learnMore:
Why keep SBOMs

An SBOM is a snapshot of the contents of a release. Keeping each one means a new report about an old version can be answered by a search, without rebuilding anything.

Common mistake

Generating an SBOM at build time, scanning it once, and discarding it.
items.reflection: Think of an inventory you could search the day bad news arrives. What would you have to reconstruct if you had never written it down?

items.prompt: Why is an SBOM scanned again after a release has shipped?
choices: Package files change on disk after deployment
New problems get published about shipped versions
The SBOM format expires after a fixed number of days
Scanning at build time is usually skipped to save time
items.explanation: The contents are fixed, but what is known about them keeps changing.

with stored SBOMs: search by name and version
new problem published later: re-scan every stored SBOM

Whether a package is present in a release

items.explanation: It lists contents; deciding whether they are hostile needs a scanner or a reviewer.

items.prompt: Implement `isCaret(range)`: return `true` if the range starts with `^`, otherwise `false`.
items.explanation: A caret range begins with the caret character, so a prefix test is enough.

items.prompt: Implement `isWildcard(range)`: return `true` for `"*"` or the empty string, otherwise `false`.
items.explanation: Both a star and an empty range allow any version, so either counts.

items.prompt: Implement `isExactPin(range)`: return `true` only if the range is three dot-separated numbers like `"1.2.0"` with no prefix.
items.explanation: An exact pin has no prefix character and all three number parts.

items.prompt: Implement `purl(name, version)` returning a package URL in the form `pkg:npm/<name>@<version>`.
items.explanation: A package URL is a fixed prefix, the name, an at sign and the version.

items.prompt: Implement `hasPostinstall(scripts)`: `scripts` is an object of script names to commands. Return `true` if it has a `postinstall` key.
items.explanation: A new postinstall key is exactly the signal a bump review looks for.

items.prompt: Implement `majorOf(version)`: return the major number of a version string like `"2.4.1"` as a number.
items.explanation: Split on dots, take the first part, and convert it to a number.

items.prompt: Implement `executions(ciRunsPerDay, days)`: the number of times a hostile install script runs.
items.explanation: Runs are installs per day multiplied by the days the version stays undetected.

items.prompt: Implement `driftCount(total, loosePercent)`: how many of `total` packages are loose, rounded to a whole number.
items.explanation: Multiply total by the percentage and divide by 100, rounding to a whole package.

items.prompt: Implement `findLooseNames(node)`. A node is `{ name, range, dependencies }`; the root has `range: null` and is never reported. A range is loose if it starts with `^`, `~` or `*`, or is empty. Return the names of loose nodes anywhere in the tree, parents before their children.

tests.expr: expect(findLooseNames({ name: "app", range: null, dependencies: [ { name: "ledger-pdf", range: "^3.1.0", dependencies: [ { name: "case-fold", range: "^2.0.0", dependencies: [] }, { name: "font-metrics", range: "1.2.0", dependencies: [] } ] } ] })).toEqual(["ledger-pdf","case-fold"])
expect(findLooseNames({ name: "app", range: null, dependencies: [{ name: "x", range: "*", dependencies: [] }] })).toEqual(["x"])

items.explanation: Check the node itself, then recurse into each child. The root has a null range, so it is skipped, and an empty child list contributes nothing.
items.reference:
A range says how far an install may move
1.2.0: exactly this version
~1.2.0: patch drift
^1.2.0: minor and patch drift
* or empty: anything
340 x 85% = 289 packages may drift
Why: every loose range is a place where a change can arrive without a diff.
items.learnMore:
Reading ranges

A caret or tilde range lets a fresh install pick a newer version of the package without any file changing. Walking the tree and reporting each loose range, with its depth, shows where that can happen.

Common mistake

Looking only at your own package.json; the loose ranges are often written in other packages' files.
items.reflection: Think of a standing instruction that says 'use the newest one'. Where in your work does that quietly let something change without a record?

items.prompt: Implement `maxLooseDepth(node)`. The root is depth 0 and has `range: null`. A range is loose if it starts with `^`, `~` or `*`, or is empty. Return the greatest depth of any loose node, or -1 if there is none.

tests.expr: expect(maxLooseDepth({ name: "app", range: null, dependencies: [ { name: "ledger-pdf", range: "^3.1.0", dependencies: [ { name: "case-fold", range: "^2.0.0", dependencies: [] }, { name: "font-metrics", range: "1.2.0", dependencies: [] } ] } ] })).toBe(2)
expect(maxLooseDepth({ name: "app", range: null, dependencies: [{ name: "x", range: "1.0.0", dependencies: [] }] })).toBe(-1)
expect(maxLooseDepth({ name: "app", range: null, dependencies: [{ name: "x", range: "~1.0.0", dependencies: [{ name: "y", range: "2.0.0", dependencies: [] }] }] })).toBe(1)

items.explanation: Start with this node's own depth if it is loose, otherwise -1, then take the maximum over every child searched one level deeper.

A range says how far an install may move
1.2.0: exactly this version
~1.2.0: patch drift
^1.2.0: minor and patch drift
* or empty: anything
340 x 85% = 289 packages may drift
Why: every loose range is a place where a change can arrive without a diff.

Common mistake

items.prompt: Implement `countLooseTransitive(node)`. The root is depth 0 and has `range: null`; depth 1 nodes are direct dependencies. A range is loose if it starts with `^`, `~` or `*`, or is empty. Count loose nodes at depth 2 or deeper (the transitive ones).

tests.expr: expect(countLooseTransitive({ name: "app", range: null, dependencies: [ { name: "ledger-pdf", range: "^3.1.0", dependencies: [ { name: "case-fold", range: "^2.0.0", dependencies: [] }, { name: "font-metrics", range: "1.2.0", dependencies: [] } ] } ] })).toBe(1)
expect(countLooseTransitive({ name: "app", range: null, dependencies: [{ name: "x", range: "^1.0.0", dependencies: [] }] })).toBe(0)

expect(countLooseTransitive({ name: "app", range: null, dependencies: [{ name: "x", range: "1.0.0", dependencies: [{ name: "y", range: "^1.0.0", dependencies: [{ name: "z", range: "*", dependencies: [] }] }] }] })).toBe(2)

items.explanation: Count a node only when it is at depth 2 or more and loose, then add the counts from its children one level deeper.
items.reference:
A range says how far an install may move
1.2.0: exactly this version
~1.2.0: patch drift
^1.2.0: minor and patch drift
* or empty: anything
340 x 85% = 289 packages may drift
Why: every loose range is a place where a change can arrive without a diff.

items.prompt: What is a `postinstall` script?
choices: A backup copy of installed files
A test the registry runs on upload
Code that runs right after install
items.explanation: The installer runs it automatically, with no import needed.

items.prompt: What does `npm ci --ignore-scripts` do?
choices: Installs, skipping install scripts
Deletes the lockfile before installing
Skips downloading all dependencies
items.explanation: It installs the packages but does not run their install scripts.

items.prompt: In the default order, when do hostile install scripts run?
choices: After every check has passed
Before any checks run
Only when your code imports them
items.explanation: The install itself runs the scripts, ahead of later checks.

items.prompt: Which diff signal is the loudest red flag in a version bump?
choices: A longer changelog entry
A new patch version number
A new postinstall script
items.explanation: It adds code that runs automatically.

items.prompt: Why is a new install script riskier than new library code?
choices: It runs before any of your own code
It is always larger in size
It is stored in a different registry
items.explanation: Library code waits to be used; an install script does not.

items.prompt: Does `--ignore-scripts` in CI protect a developer's laptop?
choices: Yes, settings sync through the registry
No, it only affects that CI step
Yes, it is stored in the lockfile
items.explanation: The flag applies where it is set.

items.prompt: What should run first in a safer CI order?
choices: Run the scripts, then verify
Deploy to staging, then verify the install
Install without scripts, then verify
items.explanation: Verification has to happen before scripts are allowed.

items.prompt: Does ignoring scripts make a package trustworthy?
choices: No, it only delays when code can run
Yes, hostile code needs scripts to work
Yes, the registry re-checks it
items.explanation: The package can still run its code once your program imports it.

items.prompt: Northfield's CI runs install, then an integrity check, then a scan. When does a hostile `postinstall` script run relative to those checks?
choices: After the integrity check but before the scan
After both checks, and only if they pass
During the install, before either check runs
Never, because CI always runs checks first
items.explanation: The install runs the script, so it precedes every later step.
items.reference:
Which comes first?
default: install, scripts run, then checks
safer: install without scripts, verify, scan, then allow scripts
a new postinstall in a bump diff: new code that runs before yours
Why: a script cannot do harm in a step where it does not run.
items.learnMore:
Order of operations in CI

Checks that run after the install cannot stop code the install already ran. Installing without scripts, verifying, and only then allowing scripts reorders the risk. It protects the CI step it is set in, not other machines.

Common mistake

Believing a flag in one CI job protects laptops, other jobs, or the package once your own code runs it.
items.reflection: Think of a process where the safety check happens after the risky step. What would moving the check earlier cost?

items.prompt: CI installs with `--ignore-scripts`, but a teammate runs a plain install locally. What is true?

The laptop is covered once the lockfile is committed
The laptop is covered because CI passed first
The teammate's laptop can still run the script
items.explanation: The flag lives in the CI step; it does not travel with the package or the lockfile.

items.prompt: What does the typosquat check measure?
choices: Edit distance between two names
How many people download a package
How old the repository is
items.explanation: It compares a candidate name with popular names.

items.prompt: What is the edit distance between `csae-fold` and `case-fold`?
items.explanation: Two letters are out of place, so two edits.

items.prompt: Would the typosquat check flag the real `case-fold` after a takeover?
choices: Yes, any new version is flagged
Yes, takeovers change the name
No, its name is exactly right
items.explanation: A takeover keeps the real name, so the distance is zero.

items.prompt: What does a silent detector mean?
choices: Its attack shape was not present
The system is safe
Another detector must have fired
items.explanation: It only says the shape it looks for was not found.

items.prompt: Which defence catches different bytes served by a mirror?
choices: Typosquat distance check
Lockfile integrity hash
Dependency scanning
items.explanation: The hash is a fingerprint of the content.

items.prompt: Why use several checks together?
choices: Together they cost less to maintain
One check is always enough
Each one catches a different shape
items.explanation: No single check covers every attack shape.

items.prompt: Which step is best at catching a new `postinstall` script?
choices: A person reading the version diff
The integrity hash comparison on install
The typosquat distance check
items.explanation: Only a reader of the diff sees what was added.

items.prompt: When does an SBOM do its best work in the Northfield story?
choices: Before publish, to stop the hostile release
After detection, finding affected releases
During install, to stop the script
items.explanation: It answers which releases contain the package.

items.prompt: The typosquat check reports nothing for a hijacked, correctly named package. How should that silence be read?
choices: Its shape was absent; other shapes are still unchecked
The package is safe, since the name is right
The package is probably safe, since no one has reported it
The scanner and the hash check can be switched off
items.explanation: Silence reports on one shape only. A takeover is a different shape.
items.reference:
Each check sees one shape
integrity hash: swapped bytes
typosquat distance: look-alike names
scanner: published problems
bump review: new scripts, new publishers
a silent check means its shape was absent
Why: run several checks, because no single one covers every shape.
items.learnMore:
Reading silence correctly

A detector built for one attack shape reports nothing when another shape is present. The real `case-fold` has distance zero from itself, so a look-alike check passes it however hostile the new release is.

Common mistake

Treating a quiet dashboard as a safe system.
items.reflection: Think of an alarm that has never gone off. What kinds of problem could it be unable to see at all?
